VaxTrack · Federal Ministry of Health, DRIVE Initiative

Designing a vaccine supply chain for people standing in the sun

VaxTrack follows vaccines from the national store all the way to a health post with no fridge. I lead design on it: the national dashboard on the web, and the field app for the people who carry, count and receive the doses.

Role
Lead product designer
Platform
Web and Android
Timeline
May 2026 to now
Users
9 roles, 4 levels
vaxtrack.org ↗Google Play ↗
The starting point

Before VaxTrack, moving vaccines from a state store to a clinic ran on handwritten registers and phone calls. Nobody had a live picture of where a dose was.

So when something went wrong, people found out late. When I wrote the PRD, I listed the things that actually happen today. Every one of them is a vaccine that never reaches a child.

  1. 01Stockouts nobody seesA facility runs out of a vaccine and the state store finds out weeks later.
  2. 02Deliveries nobody can proveThe driver says the vaccines were delivered. The facility says they never came. There's no proof either way.
  3. 03Fridges that fail at nightA fridge stops working overnight. By morning the vaccines are ruined and nobody was alerted.
  4. 04Stock in the wrong placeOne facility holds more than it can use before expiry while the one down the road has run out of the same vaccine.
Who it's for

Nine roles, one record of every dose.

Vaccines move down four levels and requests move up. Every screen in VaxTrack belongs to someone at a specific point in that chain, and each person only sees their part of it.

LevelWhoWhat they need from VaxTrack
NationalNational officer, SLWG memberSee every state at once and approve how vaccines are shared out
StateState cold chain store officerReceive from national and send down to LGAs and facilities
LGALGA cold chain store officerHold stock and supply the facilities around it
FacilityEHF in-charge, UHF in-chargeConfirm what arrived, log doses used, keep stock honest
On the road3PL, MCCO, conveyorMove the vaccines and prove every handoff
The turning point

My first PRD had eight users. The field had nine.

The PRD I wrote in June assumed health posts without a fridge would request vaccines in the app, like every other facility. Talking it through with the programme team showed me that's not how it works. The in-charge tells a conveyor what they need, in person. The conveyor collects the doses from the equipped facility that serves the health post on the morning of the session, delivers them, and brings back whatever wasn't used.

That person wasn't in my PRD at all. By the time I wrote the field user guide in July, the conveyor had their own journey in both directions, and the health post's app had shrunk to two jobs: confirm what arrived and keep a history.

Designing for the field

A budget Android, one hand and no signal.

The 3PL and the MCCO do most of their work standing outside a facility, often in direct sun, on a mid-range or budget Android, sometimes with one hand free and a low battery. Network drops in a lot of delivery areas. English isn't everyone's first language. That shaped almost every decision in the field app.

  1. 01One job per screenEvery primary action is a full-width button at the bottom, in words a tired person can't misread. Start trip. I have arrived. Next, quality check.
  2. 02Numbers you can read in the sunCounts and doses are set large in a monospaced face on high-contrast cards, so 17 never looks like 71.
  3. 03It saves itselfEverything entered stays on the phone and sends when the signal comes back. An offline indicator sits at the top so nobody has to guess.
  4. 04One colour languageRed means act now, amber means pay attention soon, green means fine, grey means history. It means the same thing on a phone at a health post and on the national dashboard.
The field app

Following one delivery.

From the state store to a health post with no fridge.

01

Deliver

A delivery needs two people to close it. The 3PL carries the vaccines. The MCCO is the government's accountability officer on every trip. Neither of them can mark a delivery as done alone, and that rule came straight from the programme.

  • Nearest expiry firstFirst expiry, first out is a programme rule, so every batch list on the manifest is sorted by expiry date, soonest at the top.
  • A shortfall doesn't stop the tripIf the count is short, the MCCO enters what actually arrived and why. The delivery can still close and the gap goes on record for the store to follow up.
  • The 3PL can see the MCCO workingWhile the count happens, the 3PL's screen says verification is in progress, then MCCO verified. Nobody is standing around asking if they're done.
02

Receive

An equipped health facility has its own fridge, so it holds stock. Their in-charge doesn't place routine orders. Their job is to confirm what arrives, log what gets used and hand vaccines to the conveyor.

  • What's running out comes firstStock is sorted by urgency, with a word on every status as well as a colour. Stockout, critical, low, OK.
  • The three things they actually doLog doses, dispense to the conveyor, authorise a return. They sit above everything else as big tiles.
  • Nothing leaves without a codeDispensing gives the in-charge a one-time code to show the conveyor. Until it's entered on their phone, the vaccines haven't left the facility's stock.
03

Last mile

The leg I didn't know existed when I started. The conveyor takes vaccines from an equipped facility to a health post for one session, and brings back what wasn't used, all in the same day.

  • The health post just confirmsNo fridge means no stock to manage. The UHF app opens on what's coming and one button to say it arrived.
  • Returns can't come before collectionThe return step stays locked until the forward leg is submitted. You can't log a return for vaccines that never went out.
  • The app does the vial mathsDiluents and syringes fill in by themselves, and quantities have to match full vials, so a wrong number gets caught while the conveyor is still typing.
The national view

1,759 facilities, one screen.

The national officer needs the opposite of the field app: everything at once. The dashboard opens on eight numbers the programme measures itself by, each with its target and a plain label for how far off it is. Under that is every vaccine across every state, where a red cell means zero doses.

Design system

So nine apps still feel like one.

I built the VaxTrack design system in Figma alongside the screens, with light and dark modes from the start. On top of the usual colour scales and semantic tokens, there's a set of tokens for the supply chain itself. A stock-out badge on the national dashboard and one on a facility phone pull from the same place.

Shipping it

The store listing and the user guide.

I designed the Play Store graphics, and wrote the user guide field staff use. One section per role, numbered steps, and nothing they'd need a dictionary for.

Looking back

What I'd do next.

  1. 01Chase programme answers before screens

    The biggest changes came from answers to questions in my PRD, like how health posts actually get their vaccines. I'd push to get those answers before drawing anything.

  2. 02Watch it used at a real stop

    Everything in the field app was designed for sun, one hand and bad network. I want to stand next to a 3PL and an MCCO at a real delivery and see what still slows them down.

  3. 03Get the cold chain alerts right

    A fridge failure destroys vaccines for good. When a temperature alert fires, it has to take over the screen, and that's the flow I most want to get right.

The lesson

My first PRD missed a whole person. Now I keep asking who actually carries the thing.
